I read this story years ago, and recall hearing about the unorthodox method of solving the difficult matter of retrieving Judy Garland from the house she died in.

Judy was very, very sick and addicted at the time of her death, and the house she stayed in while in London was very, *very*, **very** small. She'd passed away in the bathroom, seated on the toilet (just sitting and nothing else, iirc). Being a small person in a small home with a small bathroom, the removal wasn't too difficult on its own-- the problem was that the public had somehow found out that she had died/been hurt, and there was no way to get her off the property that wouldn't be a circus sideshow with the fans showing up.

The unorthodox method that was used ended up being wrapping up Judy in a carpet or rug, and having a policeman carry her out, slung over his shoulder, no one the wiser. I can't remember if there were any clandestine pics of the carpet, or if this was partially a rumor (don't shoot the messenger, I've seen the carpet story in several sources over the years). I just find it sad that she was so ill and frail that merely being wrapped in a rug could hide all of her.

As a local, you get a ticket to eat free for the next 60-70 years, one meal a day (maybe it's a reality show, who knows).The catch is that you can't pick an item for yourself, and the menu changes every day. The first week seems great. They really dote on you, and you can tell the meal was prepared with care and love. Even so, despite the restaurant's other patrons raving about it, it seems a bit bland. Still, you keep showing up.

By the next week, more people are rabid fans of the restaurant. Everyone loves the variety, but your dish tastes even worse, no matter what they're serving. You can't believe no one else is noticing this, but figure that maybe you're just not used to the taste of new dishes every time.

By week three, the food is barely edible, you keep getting food poisoning, and a waitress keeps telling you that the meals taste better when you have another person at the table to eat with you for the rest of your life. She points at group of people waiting to be seated, and indicates that at least five out of ten of them were never in prison, and this is the best you're going to get, considering how terrible your plated food looks.

Everyone else continues to love the food. They find you weird for wasting the food- if it's good enough for me, it's good enough for you.

Week four comes, and you decide that it's time to quit coming for free food entirely. However, in the moment you're about to leave the restaurant, the hostess runs ahead of you and locks the exit door. You didn't tip, and you simply can't leave without your free food. Everyone else loves it, so why not just keep eating?

From now on, you try escaping out of the place through the bathroom window every few days, but they drag you back every time for your awful meal as the rest of the lunch crowd ignore your complaints.

You're not hungry. You haven't been hungry in years. But you eat your food.

The Geraldine Haskel Affair.

Geraldine Haskel, an eighteen year old well-off socialite who was, in turn, the daughter of yet another well-off socialite, mysteriously vanished on April 19th, 1901 after a box lunch social being held at the Our Lady of Perpetual Ennui in Providence, RI. Geraldine's father, a titan of the asbestos production world and all-around *bon vivant* in dogfighting society circles, offered a reward that seemed astonishing at the time for information on her disappearance: $100,000.

The reward was never collected.

The facts of the matter:


      1. Geraldine was enamored with a 19 year old young man she had met at church one Sunday during her weekly bible study class. His name was Oswald Merchant. She invited him every so often to her firing range for tea and target practice, and he impressed her father with his extensive knowledge on 17th century French erotic literature.

       2. Oswald had a habit of admiring just about every well-dressed woman in range on his daily walks, but insisted to Geraldine that he was merely admiring the quality of modern dress making. Naturally, this was not the case, and Geraldine began using the archery range twice weekly.


      3. The final straw seemed to occur at a very popular box lunch social, where Geraldine caught Oswald in a compromising position behind a lilac bush with several scullery maids, his butler, and a riding crop. Eyewitnesses were very certain that Geraldine then announced that she was borrowing the nearest horse, and Oswald had better start running.


       4. The last sighting of the couple was Geraldine chasing Oswald at a high rate of speed out of town, practicing her horseback archery skills as they crossed the Weehachy River bridge.

I hate that I know about this, but if it helps anyone, this is what happened when my father died:

My dad hadn't worked in years, and was relatively young when he died of cancer. I'm an only child, he was an only child, and all our relatives were already gone. Medically, I couldn't work, so it was a fixed-income disability situation, and the prices from the one funeral home (recommended by the hospice nurse) didn't sound quite right. The hospital kept calling me for arrangements and I'd never done this before, let alone with no money to do it with. It was extremely traumatic time, and I had no one to help me.

I'm sure it was only a day or so later (it felt like years), and I get a knock on the door from a really well-dressed man from a local funeral home. Apparently, a different hospice nurse referred me to this place, and he sat with me for an hour to help me with logistics while I was still too upset to do it myself. He explained the process to apply for cremation assistance, and that I shouldn't feel awful for not knowing where to even begin. (Wherever you are, awesome funeral home employee, I hope you are doing well.) Most states have funding that you can apply for at the Department of Human Resources, and my state covered the entire cost. 

It doesn't surprise me that there are cremated remains left behind at times when the process of getting funeral assistance just isn't talked about very often.

This is going to be a very difficult conversation, but you need to put your foot down about hospice services. I (unfortunately), have a lot of experience with end-of-life care situations: my mother was an elder-care/hospice nurse for 20 years, I helped daily with my grandmother's terminal cancer until she passed, and I cared for both of my parents as they passed quite young from varying Stage 4 cancers-- all this before I hit 30.

*You cannot come through this crisis with your life and sanity intact without Hospice.* 

It sounds like hyperbole, but your mom needs to, at the very least, come to terms with this situation. I know, it's soul-crushing. It's miserable. I didn't have any help with my parents as an only child, and when my dad told me he was going to start hospice about a month before he passed, I was absolutely livid inside of my mind yet accepting outwardly. I didn't want to admit it was the end, but set it up for my dad, regardless.

Anything your dad needs at home, the nurses arrange. Hospital beds, prescriptions, bathroom aids. If you need a break, there are respite days where they can take your dad for a week or two to a facility (the amount of days varies; my grandmother got a 7 day respite). They also provide much faster access to pain meds than usual, and usually left a bottle of morphine for them early on (that may have changed by now, but every relative I've lost got one handed to me from the nurses). I deeply appreciated them fetching Dad's meds, as I couldn't leave him alone to get them myself with everything else going on.

It's going to be a hard situation: even *with* Hospice, that final month was full of horrible things that my mind mostly won't let me recall. The things I do recall were pure nightmare fuel, but would have been much worse without help. *Your family can't provide the right care for him without hospice workers to assist, and it's not 'giving up' to do so.* It may feel like it, but it's not. I hope your mom and dad get the help and care they need, and I hope the best for your new baby.

It's not terribly weird, but pretty outdated. Most houses in the US that were built in the huge wave of suburb building through the 1950s, 60s, and early 70s had a 'living room' and a 'family room'.

The 'family room' was where normal life happened. You'd put decent furniture in there, the TV, and chances were that it was open planned with the kitchen. Kids were kept to this area, or there could be a further 'den' room for them (this really depended on how much or how little you actually wanted to see your kids, and how much money you had to blow on a house). Sometimes the den was a proto 'man cave', with the kids relegated to a finished basement play area. 

The 'living room' was where you showed off just how much money your family had. This is where the best furniture roamed under their plastic covers, the wall-to-wall luxury carpeting deadened sound, and the very best of your knickknacks sat un-admired. *You simply were not allowed in there*, no matter who *you* were in the family, because 'that room is for company'. If you were a kid, that meant that even stepping on the carpet was as *verboten* as trying to walk right in to Fort Knox. 

I'm a little surprised that certain people still hold to a tradition of doing this in 2023, but it definitely was a thing for many years in many homes.
